## Purpose

This SOP describes the field determination of soil color using the
Munsell Soil Color Charts. Soil color is one of the most readily
observable soil properties and provides information about organic
matter content, drainage and aeration status, mineralogy, and degree
of weathering [@munsell2009; @schoeneberger2012]. Lower values (darker
soils) generally reflect higher organic matter content, especially in A
horizons, while high chroma indicates well-drained, oxidized conditions
and low chroma suggests prolonged saturation or reducing environments
[@shields1966; @lynn2009]. Red and yellow hues are controlled primarily
by iron oxide mineralogy: hematite produces redder hues (5YR and
redder), while goethite produces yellowish-brown hues (7.5YR--10YR)
[@schwertmann1993; @torrent1983]. Consistent color determination is
essential for soil profile descriptions
([SOP-F407](SOP-F407-soil-profile-description.qmd)), wetland
delineation, and site characterization.


## Scope

- **Applies to:** Field determination of soil color for all EA Program
  soil sampling campaigns, profile descriptions, and site
  characterizations
- **Does not apply to:** Instrumental color measurement (colorimeters
  or spectrophotometers); rock or sediment color classification using
  the Rock Color Chart; Munsell readings on dried, ground samples in
  the lab (see [SOP-L419](../lab_sops/SOP-L419-soil-color-munsell.qmd))
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites; can also be performed on
  fresh samples in the lab


## Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Ensure Munsell charts are available and in good condition |
| Trained Personnel | Determine soil color per this SOP                       |
| New Students      | Complete training and inter-observer calibration exercise |

## Definitions

- **Chroma:** The colorimetric purity or saturation of a color; the
  third component of Munsell notation (e.g., the 4 in 10YR 4/4); low
  chroma (2 or less) in subsurface horizons indicates gleying and
  periodic waterlogging.
- **Gleying:** A reduction process in waterlogged soils that depletes
  iron and produces low-chroma (gray, blue-gray, or green-gray) matrix
  colors; a diagnostic indicator of hydric soil conditions.
- **Hue:** The dominant spectral color in Munsell notation (e.g.,
  10YR, 7.5YR, 2.5Y, Gley 1); the first element of a Munsell
  designation; corresponds to the dominant wavelength of reflected
  light.
- **Matrix color:** The dominant color occupying more than 50% of the
  exposed soil face; recorded first in the Munsell notation before
  mottles or redoximorphic features.
- **Mottle:** A spot or blotch of color contrasting with the matrix
  color; described by abundance (few, common, many), size (fine,
  medium, coarse), and contrast (faint, distinct, prominent).
- **Munsell color system:** A standardized three-dimensional color
  notation (Hue Value/Chroma) used universally in soil science for
  objective color description; readings must be made in consistent
  natural or reference lighting conditions.
- **Redoximorphic features:** Color patterns caused by reduction and
  oxidation of iron and manganese under fluctuating saturation;
  include masses (concentrations of iron oxides) and depletions
  (zones of low chroma); diagnostic for hydric soil identification
  and wetland delineation.
- **Value:** The lightness or darkness of a color in Munsell notation;
  ranges from 0 (black) to 10 (white); the second component of
  Munsell notation (e.g., the 4 in 10YR 4/4).
  
## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Biological:** Soil-borne pathogens; wash hands after handling soil.
- **Physical:** Standard field hazards (ticks, snakes, heat exposure).
- **Chemical:** At contaminated sites, soil may contain heavy metals or
  other hazardous materials; wear gloves.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (recommended)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd).


## Equipment and Materials

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Munsell Soil Color Charts (current edition) | Handle with clean, dry hands; protect from rain and direct soil contact |
| Trowel or soil knife                  | For exposing fresh soil surfaces         |
| Squeeze bottle with DI water          | For moistening dry samples               |
| Paper towels                          | For cleaning hands between samples       |
| Field notebook                        | For recording colors                     |


## Background: The Munsell System

Munsell color notation has three components [@munsell2009;
@soilsurveystaff2022]:

- **Hue:** The dominant spectral color (e.g., 10YR, 2.5Y, 5YR).
  Pages in the chart book are arranged by hue.
- **Value:** Lightness, from 0 (absolute black) to 10 (absolute white).
  Vertical axis on each page.
- **Chroma:** Color intensity or saturation, from 0 (neutral gray)
  outward. Horizontal axis on each page.

A complete Munsell notation is written as: **Hue Value/Chroma**
(e.g., 10YR 4/3). The corresponding color name (e.g., "brown" or
"dark yellowish brown") is listed on each chip.


## Procedure

### Sample Preparation

1. Expose a fresh soil surface by breaking a ped or cutting with a
   trowel. Do not use smeared or scraped surfaces, as smearing
   compresses the soil and alters the apparent color.
2. Determine color on **moist** soil. If the soil is dry, add a few
   drops of DI water to a small subsample and allow it to absorb for
   30 seconds before reading.
3. If both moist and dry colors are needed (e.g., for profile
   descriptions), read the moist color first, then allow a portion
   to air-dry and read the dry color.

### Reading the Color

1. Work in natural daylight, ideally under an overcast sky or in
   open shade. Avoid direct sunlight on the soil or the chart, as
   glare distorts color perception. Do not read colors under
   artificial light or at twilight.
2. Hold the soil sample behind the chart page apertures so that the
   soil is visible through the holes.
3. Compare the soil to the color chips [@schoeneberger2012]. Start
   with the hue page that appears closest, then move to the value row
   that matches, then slide along the chroma axis.
4. Select the chip that most closely matches the soil. If the soil
   falls between two chips, record the notation of the nearest chip
   and note "between X and Y" in the field notebook.
5. Record the full Munsell notation and the color name:
   - Example: **10YR 3/2 (very dark grayish brown)**
6. If the soil contains mottles or redoximorphic features, record the
   matrix color and then the mottle color(s) separately, noting the
   abundance (few, common, many), size (fine, medium, coarse), and
   contrast (faint, distinct, prominent).

### Special Cases

**Organic soils (O horizons, peat):** Use the Gley pages or the 10YR
page with very low value and chroma. Very dark colors (value 2 or
less) are common.

**Gleyed soils:** Use the Gley 1 and Gley 2 pages for soils with
chroma of 2 or less and hues bluer than 5Y. Gleyed colors indicate
prolonged saturation and reducing conditions.

**Mottled soils:** Record:

- Matrix color (dominant color occupying more than 50% of the surface)
- Mottle colors (each distinct color)
- For each mottle: abundance, size, and contrast

| Abundance | Definition                          |
|:----------|:------------------------------------|
| Few       | < 2% of exposed surface             |
| Common    | 2--20% of exposed surface            |
| Many      | > 20% of exposed surface            |

| Size      | Definition                          |
|:----------|:------------------------------------|
| Fine      | < 5 mm diameter                     |
| Medium    | 5--15 mm diameter                    |
| Coarse    | > 15 mm diameter                    |

| Contrast  | Definition                          |
|:----------|:------------------------------------|
| Faint     | Hue, value, and chroma differ by 1 unit or less from matrix |
| Distinct  | Differ by 2--3 units in value or chroma |
| Prominent | Differ by more than 3 units         |

Redoximorphic features are diagnostic for hydric soil identification
and wetland delineation; consistent recording of mottle properties is
critical for regulatory applications [@soilsurveystaff2017].


## Quality Control

- At the start of each field season, have two or more observers
  independently read the same soil samples to assess inter-observer
  agreement. Readings should agree within one chip (one unit of value
  or chroma) in at least 80% of comparisons.
- Replace Munsell charts when color chips are faded, soiled, or
  damaged. Faded chips produce systematic errors.
- Record lighting conditions (overcast, open shade, sunny) in the
  field notebook; lighting affects color perception.
- Always specify whether the reading was on moist or dry soil.

Digital colorimeters and smartphone-based color apps are increasingly
used as supplements to visual Munsell matching; however, instrument
readings and visual assessments can disagree, especially at low chroma
and low value, so visual Munsell determination remains the standard
for USDA soil survey and regulatory work [@viscarra2006].

## Training Record

Before determining soil color independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Complete an inter-observer calibration exercise with a trained
   operator, achieving agreement within one chip on at least 8 of 10
   test samples
3. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
